title: I used Sprite Fusion to animate my C++ survivor game.
author: BootSudden5485
selftext:
*Hey everyone! I'm the solo dev building PIXELVIVOR, an open-world bullet-heaven roguelike running on a custom C++20 / Raylib engine (with an instant 2D ↔ 3D HD-2D camera toggle).*



*One of my biggest bottlenecks as a solo dev has always been animation—I had 18 unique biome bosses (from desert pharaohs and ice titans to underground cave wyrms and an abyssal kraken) and tons of mobs sitting around as static PNGs, and hand-animating 8-frame sheets for all of them would have taken me months.*

*I ended up hooking up Sprite Fusion (via its MCP server directly inside my dev environment) to batch-animate all 18 bosses and over half my regular mobs into 8-frame spritesheets, then wired them straight into my engine's JSON asset manifest. The biggest lesson I learned from prompting the animations was how much the motion wording matters: early tests with vague prompts like "hovering and pulsing" gave me super clean idle loops, but the boss looked like it was sliding across the map in-game. Switching to explicit locomotion prompts (alternating footsteps, wing flaps, S-wave slithering, writhing tentacles) completely fixed it and made them feel alive right away.*

*If you want to try it out, there's a browser-playable demo on itch.io (note: the web build is my earlier JS version while I work on compiling the new C++20 3D build to WebAssembly): https://pixelvivor.itch.io/pixelvivor-demo*

*Curious how other solo devs here handle consistency across a big roster of AI-animated sprites—do you stick to a single 8-frame walk/move loop per enemy, or generate separate idle/attack sheets too?*
